title: under the water and back up
hook: a baby in a white gown, a teenager in a pool: same word, an old disagreement

segments.voice: Yesterday: born again, born from above. Today, the water many churches tie to that new birth.

A baby in a long white gown, a little water poured over her head while the grandparents take photos. A teenager in a T-shirt, held by the shoulders and leaned back into a pool, coming up to cheering. Same word for both: baptism. Same faith. And a disagreement, centuries old, about when and how to do it. Both sides have their reasons.
screen: `A WHITE GOWN.` → `A T-SHIRT, A POOL.` → `SAME WORD.`

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, to plunge, to immerse. It's older than the church. A wild preacher named John was dipping people in the Jordan River as a sign of turning their lives around, and Jesus himself walked into that river and was baptized. Later he sent his friends out to baptize, and from the start, baptism was how someone joined. So why two pictures? Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize babies. The idea: God's promise comes first, before the child can answer, and the family promises to raise them in it. Baptist, Pentecostal and many non-denominational churches baptize people old enough to say yes for themselves, usually all the way under. Paul's picture fits that well: down into the water like a burial, up like rising from the dead. Whether baptism itself saves is a real difference too. Many churches call it the moment God makes a person new. Many others call it an outward sign of something God has already done inside. Either way, the shape is the same.
screen: `BAPTIZO — TO DIP, TO PLUNGE.` · `JOHN, THE JORDAN, JESUS.` · `BABIES, OR THOSE WHO CHOOSE.` · `A SIGN, OR THE MOMENT ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, breathe all the way out, slowly, like going under. On the second, pause a moment in the stillness before you breathe in. On the third, breathe in deep, like coming up into the air. Notice how that first breath feels.
Baptism. From the Greek for dip or plunge: the way into the church, with water. Fourth word.
Your line: under the water, up again. A white gown or a T-shirt in a pool, it's the same picture. Day four.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize infants (by pouring, sprinkling or, in Orthodox churches, immersion); Baptist, Pentecostal and many non-denominational churches baptize believers, usually by full immersion. Almost all baptize once, in water, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

what a scholar hears: baptizo, to dip or immerse; Romans 6:3–4 reads it as burial and resurrection; infant and believer's baptism have divided churches since the Anabaptists of the 1520s.

story.title: the chariot on the desert road
story.text: A powerful official is riding home in a chariot, reading out loud from the prophet Isaiah and not understanding it. A stranger named Philip runs up alongside and asks: do you understand what you're reading? The official invites him up, and they talk as the chariot rolls down the desert road. Then they pass some water. The official says: look, here is water; what's stopping me from being baptized? They stop the chariot, go down into the water together, and he goes on his way rejoicing.

wrong.myth: all churches baptize the same way, at the same age.
wrong.truth: some baptize babies, by pouring or sprinkling or dipping; some baptize people old enough to choose, usually all the way under. both trace it to Jesus.

notes: New lesson (2026-10-06), written from the audience research: baptism (top-20 moment 4, proposed day 4), modeling 'different churches do this differently' without picking a side.

Which churches baptize infants (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist, Presbyterian) and which baptize believers (Baptist, Pentecostal, many non-denominational) is generalized; there are exceptions (e.g. some Methodists and non-denominational churches do both). Confirm.

'Whether baptism saves': 'many churches call it the moment God makes a person new' (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and others; Churches of Christ in their own way); 'many others call it an outward sign' (Baptists and many evangelicals). Confirm each would recognize itself.
Paul's burial-and-rising picture (Romans 6:3–4) is paraphrased; 'fits that well' does not claim Paul taught immersion only.
Story card: the Ethiopian official (Acts 8). The voice of verse 37 (found in later manuscripts) is not used.
